metaDescription: Four iDPRT thermal label printers compared on ips, dpi, label width and connectivity: the iD880, the SP310, a 3 inch LAN unit and a wireless 4x6 model.
expertTake: The iD880 is the best iDPRT for most sellers because it prints a 4x6 label in about a second, takes label widths from 1 to 4.64 inches and offers both USB and Ethernet. The SP310 is the pick for address, FBA and file labels on narrower stock. Anyone who ships from a phone only should look at the wireless 4x6 model, and anyone who needs ribbon-grade durability should skip this brand's direct thermal printers entirely.
introParagraphs: A newer group of thermal printer makers has built a following with online sellers by pairing a fast engine with open label stock and a simple driver. These printers skip the ribbon, accept third-party labels and aim at the packing bench rather than the industrial dock.

What to compare is width range, speed, how the printer connects and how well the drivers cover your operating system. Those four points decide whether a printer fits a small shipping operation or becomes a weekly nuisance.

products.name: iDPRT iD880 4x6 direct thermal printer, 6 ips, USB and Ethernet
products.description:
Width flexibility gives the iD880 an edge over fixed 4x6 machines. It accepts labels from 1 inch to 4.64 inches wide, so a seller can print a parcel label in the morning and a narrow product label in the afternoon without changing printers. The listing describes it as a commercial-grade direct thermal desktop printer for high-volume operations.

Speed is up to 6 inches per second at 203 dpi, which the maker says prints a standard 4x6 label in about one second. That figure assumes a short data job and a fast host, so treat it as a ceiling. Both a USB cable and an Ethernet cord are included, and the driver downloads through a QR code, which keeps setup short. Compared with the SP310 and the 3 inch unit, this is the widest and fastest of the three wired models.

As with every direct thermal machine, label fade is the cost of convenience. Keep finished labels out of hot rooms, wipe the head with alcohol and stock labels that match the roll holder. A second iD880 listing in the same family adds a built-in paper compartment and USB-only connection, so check which version you are ordering.
products.bestFor: Sellers and small warehouses who print 4x6 parcel and narrower labels on one machine.
pros: Prints about one 4x6 label per second at 6 ips
USB and Ethernet in the box
cons: Printed labels dim in heat and light
Speed is a ceiling, not a sustained rate
Two listings with different connection options

products.description:
Small labels, many of them, is the job this printer is built for. It prints 2x3 inch labels at up to 80 per minute at 4 ips and 203 dpi, which the listing aims at FBA and address label work. Labels from 1 to 3.35 inches wide fit, so it cannot print a 4x6 parcel label.

The listing stresses third-party label compatibility, so you are free to buy stock from any supplier, unlike printers that read a chip on the roll. Plug-and-play USB with separate drivers for Windows, macOS, Linux and ChromeOS is a practical selling point for mixed offices, and the maker says there are no wireless dropouts, since the connection is wired.

Because it is a narrower head, labels cost less per piece, and the whole printer is smaller than the iD880. Wipe the head every few rolls, keep the roll guides snug and store labels cool. If you ever need to ship a parcel, you will need a second printer, so decide on your main job before buying.

products.name: iDPRT 3 inch thermal label printer, USB and LAN
products.description:
A 3 inch machine with a LAN port fills a gap between the narrow address printer and the full 4x6 model. The listing says you can print a variety of label types over USB or the network, and it eliminates the need for ink or ribbon. For a small office where several people need address and barcode labels, the network option is the reason to consider it.

The listing makes broad claims about speed and cost savings, so judge it by its specifications and not its slogans: 3 inch width, direct thermal technology and USB or LAN. Next to the SP310, the 3 inch unit offers a network port, while the SP310 offers a published speed figure and a wide driver list. Next to the iD880, it gives up the 4x6 capability.

Treat it as a small-office printer and keep supplies simple. Wipe the head, keep guides snug and check that your label roll core fits the holder. If your volume grows, the iD880 is the natural step up.
products.bestFor: Small offices sharing a printer for address and barcode labels.

products.name: iDPRT 4x6 wireless thermal printer, HereLabel app, Bluetooth

specList.label: Carriers
specList.value: UPS and USPS via PDF download

products.description:
Printing from a phone is what this model is about. It uses the HereLabel app over Bluetooth on iPhone, Android, Windows 10 and 11, and macOS, and it also connects by USB. The listing says you can print UPS and USPS labels by downloading the standard 4x6 PDF from the carrier and sending it to the printer.

That workflow is practical for occasional sellers who do not want a desktop printer on the packing table. Against the iD880, you give up Ethernet and the extra width range, but gain a wireless workflow aimed at phones. The usual caution about Bluetooth applies: pairing can fail, range is short and the app must be kept current.

It is a direct thermal printer, so there is no ink or ribbon, and labels fade with heat. Keep a USB cable at hand, wipe the head and use 4x6 labels sized to the guides. If you ship daily, the wired iD880 will be steadier.
products.bestFor: Occasional sellers who ship from a phone or tablet.
cons: Fewer width options than the iD880

buyingCriteria.explanation: The iD880 handles 1 to 4.64 inches, the SP310 handles 1 to 3.35 inches and the 3 inch model stays within its own width class. Only the iD880 and the wireless 4x6 model print standard parcel labels. Measure your widest label before choosing, and include the liner edge, because the printable area is slightly smaller than the stated media width. A seller who also prints return labels or product tags on narrower stock should look for a printer that moves its guides smoothly, since constant resetting is where skewed prints come from. If you only ever print one size, the narrower machine is usually the better value.

The iD880 is rated up to 6 ips and the SP310 up to 4 ips, but the SP310 lists 80 small labels per minute because small labels print quickly. The two are not comparable without label length. For a mixed workload, count your real label sizes. A shop that prints three hundred 2x3 inch labels in an hour is well served by the SP310's rating, while a shop that prints three hundred parcel labels will wait on the longer 4x6 feed whatever the headline number says. Also leave headroom, since a printer working at its limit all day wears its head and roller faster.

The SP310 states it accepts third-party labels, which keeps label cost down. Printers that read a chip on the roll can lock you into the maker's stock. Always confirm label compatibility before buying a roll. Open stock also lets you shop for the best price per thousand labels and order a few sample rolls from different suppliers, since adhesive strength and paper sensitivity vary between brands. A label that prints dark but peels off a poly mailer is a worse buy than a slightly pricier one that sticks.

The iD880 and SP310 are wired, with USB and Ethernet on the iD880. The wireless 4x6 model uses Bluetooth and an app. A busy shipper is better with a wired link, while a phone-based seller may prefer the cable-free workflow. Wired connections do not care about router restarts, phone updates or battery saver settings, which is why shipping benches overwhelmingly use them. If you pick wireless, keep the app and the phone's operating system current and test a label after every update.

The SP310 lists separate drivers for Windows, macOS, Linux and ChromeOS, and the iD880 installs from a QR code download. Mixed offices need a printer whose driver actually runs on every computer. Test on your system during the return window. Install the driver, print a real label from your shipping platform and check the alignment on the first label, since a driver that installs cleanly can still shift the print by a few millimeters. If the print is off, the fix is usually a page-size setting in the shipping tool, not a faulty printer.

All of these are direct thermal, so labels fade in heat, light and time. That is fine for parcels but not for long-term tags. If you need durable labels, a ribbon printer is the right tool. Parcels that ride in a hot delivery van for a day are fine, but a product label on a boxed item that sits in a sunlit shop window will gray out over a season. Printing a spare and keeping it in a drawer is a useful way to see how your stock ages.

howWeEvaluated.title: Label size and format
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared width ranges and the label sizes each printer supports. The iD880's 1 to 4.64 inch range is the widest. The SP310 and the 3 inch model were judged as narrower tools.

howWeEvaluated.title: Speed and workload
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the stated ips and label counts per minute. The iD880 at 6 ips and the SP310 at 80 labels per minute represent different workloads. We treated them as ceilings, and we gave more weight to the stated label width range than to speed, since a printer that cannot take your label is useless however fast it is.

howWeEvaluated.title: Connectivity and drivers
howWeEvaluated.description: USB, Ethernet and Bluetooth support, plus listed operating systems, were checked. The SP310's four-platform driver list stands out. The Bluetooth model was judged on convenience and risk.

howWeEvaluated.title: Consumables and openness
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked whether the printer takes third-party labels. Direct thermal labels fade, and that was a shared limit. We did not quote prices.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership reality
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on owner feedback patterns, we weighed head cleaning, roller wear and app dependence. Wired printers scored for steadiness. Wireless models were judged for convenience against the risk of pairing issues. Because this is a newer brand with a thinner long-term record than older barcode makers, we put extra weight on how clearly each listing states its specifications and driver support.

cards.label: Wired
cards.text: The iD880 and SP310 use USB, and the iD880 adds Ethernet. They are steady and fast. They tie the printer to a desk.

cards.label: Wireless
cards.text: The 4x6 model uses Bluetooth and an app. It works from a phone. It depends on pairing and app support.

howToChoose.note: Choose wired for volume; choose wireless for phone shipping. A seller who prints more than a few dozen labels a day will feel every dropped Bluetooth link, so the cable on the iD880 or SP310 pays for itself in saved minutes.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A printer that handles your label size, accepts cheap stock and has drivers for your computer.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The iD880 covers parcels and narrow labels, the SP310 covers FBA, and the wireless 4x6 covers occasional phone shipping. The 3 inch LAN model suits a small office that mails letters and packages from several desks, and it should not be bought as a parcel printer.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You print hundreds of labels a day. The iD880 is the strongest here, because its wide label range lets it absorb a change in what you sell without a second purchase, and its Ethernet port lets a second packer share it.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You print occasionally. The wireless 4x6 model or the 3 inch unit is enough, and either one can be replaced later without regret if your volume grows into the iD880.

maintenance.why: Dust and adhesive dim prints. A swab dampened with alcohol removes them.

Residue causes misfeeds. A clean roller stops labels skewing. Use a swab damp with alcohol, rotate the roller by hand while you wipe and let it dry fully before feeding labels, because a damp roller can pull a label off its liner.

Loose guides skew prints. Snug guides keep the print on the label. After a roll change, feed one blank label and confirm it exits straight, because a roll that sits slightly crooked will drift further as it unwinds.

Operating system updates can break drivers. The Bluetooth model needs its app updated. Keep the installer file on a shared drive so a replacement computer can be set up in minutes without hunting for a download link.
Warm storage darkens thermal rolls. Keep spare rolls sealed.

faq.a: Choose the iD880 if you print 4x6 parcel labels. Choose the SP310 for address, FBA and small labels, where it prints up to 80 per minute.

It works for occasional use, but Bluetooth pairing can fail and range is short. Keep a USB cable ready as a backup, and avoid relying on it for a deadline-driven shipment where a dropped link costs you a carrier pickup.

faq.q: How durable are the printed labels?
faq.a: Labels printed this way dim in sun and heat. They suit parcels, and ribbon printers suit long-term tags. Storing spare labels in a cool cupboard and printing shortly before shipping gives the longest practical life.

faq.q: Does the iD880 come in more than one version?
faq.a: Yes. One listing is USB with a built-in paper compartment, and another adds Ethernet. Read the listing carefully before ordering, and confirm the connection options and label width range match what you expect, because the title alone does not always show the difference.
